content: The preparation of this section of the guidelines was supervised by Nazir Ismail and Alexei Korobitsyn, with contributions from Dennis Falzon, Cecily Miller, Fuad Mirzayev, Lice Gonzalez-Angulo, Anna Dean, Annabel Baddeley, and Carl-Michael Nathanson, all of whom are part of the WHO Global TB Programme. Additional input was provided by Lara Vojnov from the WHO Global HIV Programme, Mercedes Gonzalez from WHO Innovation, Access, and Use, and Soudeh Ehsani from the WHO Regional Office for Europe. The Guideline Development Group was co-chaired by Holger Schünemann, a methodologist from McMaster University in Canada, and Jeremiah Chakaya Muhwa from the International Union Against TB and Lung Diseases in Kenya. Other members included Denise Arakaki-Sanchez from the Ministry of Health in Brazil, David Branigan from the Treatment Action Group in the USA, Daniela Cirillo from the San Raffaele Supranational TB Reference Laboratory in Italy, and Celina Anna Maria Garfin from the National TB Programme in the Philippines. Additional contributors were Petra de Haas from the KNCV Tuberculosis Foundation in the Netherlands, Patricia Hall from the CDC in the USA, Rumina Hasan from Aga Khan University in Pakistan, Xia Hui from the National TB Control Programme in China, Farzana Ismail from the National Institute for Communicable Diseases in South Africa, Katharina Kranzer from LSHTM in Zimbabwe, Blessina Kumar from the Global Coalition of TB Activists in India, Nagalingeswaran Kumarasamy from YRG Care in India, Lindiwe Mvusi from the National TB Programme in South Africa, Viet Nhung Nguyen from the National TB Control Programme in Vietnam, Mark Nicol from the University of Western Australia, Leen Rigouts from the Prince Leopold Institute of Tropical Medicine in Belgium, Thomas Shinnick as an independent consultant in the USA, Hojoon Sohn from Johns Hopkins University in the USA, Sabira Tahseen from the National TB Control Programme in Pakistan, and Ezio Tavora dos Santos Filho from the Civil Society Task Force in Brazil. The External Review Group included Lucilaine Ferrazoli from Instituto Adolfo Lutz in Brazil, Alaine Umubyeyi Nyaruhirira from Management Sciences for Health in South Africa, Elisa Tagliani from the San Raffaele Supranational TB Reference Laboratory in Italy, Francis Varaine from Médecins Sans Frontières in France, and Danila Zimenkov from the Engelhardt Institute of Molecular Biology in Russia. The Systematic Review Team consisted of Mikashmi Kohli from McGill University in Canada, Samuel Schumacher from FIND in Switzerland, Karen Steingart from the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group in the USA, Grant Theron from Stellenbosch University in South Africa, Annelies Van Rie from the University of Antwerp in Belgium, Michael Whitfield from the University of Antwerp in Belgium, Alice Zwerling from the University of Ottawa in Canada, Sazia Naz from the University of Ottawa in Canada, Brianna Empringham from the University of Ottawa in Canada, Nora Engel from Maastricht University in the Netherlands, Ricky Janssen from Maastricht University in the Netherlands, and Muthoni Mwaura from Maastricht University in the Netherlands. Observers included Elie Akl from the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, Draurio Cravo Neto Barreira from Unitaid in Switzerland, Fatim Cham-Jallow from The Global Fund in Switzerland, Margaretha de Vos from FIND in Switzerland, Brian Kaiser from the Global Drug Facility in Switzerland, Gloriyah Kerubo Moses from the AYARHEP board in Kenya, Amy Piatek from USAID in the USA, Morten Ruhwald from FIND in Switzerland, Srinath Satyanarayana from the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in India, and Wayne Van Gemert from the Stop TB Partnership in Switzerland. Funding for the development of these guidelines was provided by USAID and the Russian Federation through the Russian Federation–WHO consolidated grant no. REM-RUS-030. The views of the funding agencies did not influence the development or content of these guidelines. The WHO’s End TB Strategy emphasizes the importance of early diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB) and universal drug susceptibility testing (DST). This highlights the critical role of laboratories in rapidly and accurately detecting TB and drug resistance in the post-2015 era. The WHO’s assessment process for TB diagnostics currently focuses on evaluating classes of TB diagnostic technologies rather than specific products. The guidelines include recommendations for various diagnostic technologies, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), which are widely used for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) DNA and mutations associated with rifampicin resistance. These tools, such as Xpert® MTB/RIF and Xpert® MTB/RIF Ultra, are automated and provide all-in-one solutions suitable for peripheral-level laboratories. They require established laboratory networks and trained personnel to operate effectively. Moderate-complexity automated NAATs, such as Abbott RealTime® MTB and BD MAX™ MDR-TB, are faster and less complex than phenotypic culture-based DST and line probe assays (LPAs). These tests can be used as initial diagnostic tools for detecting TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid simultaneously. They offer rapid and accurate results, making them suitable for high-population-density areas with efficient sample referral systems. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) is another diagnostic technology included in the guidelines.
